title: A baby too tired to breathe

objective: Assess and manage respiratory distress in infants and children, including croup and bronchiolitis
secondaryObjectives: Apply the clinical judgment steps to a child in respiratory distress
Recognize and manage pediatric cardiac arrest and bradycardia with poor perfusion

sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in a text extraction of the Louisiana copy (the extractor did not keep every table column, so placement was checked against the course's own reading of 2026-11-09 in ems-sources.ts). EMR: CPR and AED, tourniquet and wound packing, naloxone, oral airway, BVM, oxygen; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector, aspirin, oral glucose, CPAP, 12-lead acquisition (not interpretation), transport. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways and a limited list of IV and IM medications including dextrose and glucagon. Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, intubation and the wider formulary. No newer model was found 2026-11-11 (EMS.gov's page was unavailable; the only other 'update' found is the 2017 change notice adding tourniquets, wound packing and naloxone to EMR and EMT).

brief.situation: 02:40. You are the paramedic on an ALS ambulance with an EMT partner. Ava, 7 months, about 8 kg, has had a cold for three days; tonight she stopped feeding and her parents say she 'breathes funny'. She lies in her mother's arms, pale, eyes half closed.
handover: Ex-premature at 34 weeks; no other illness. The children's hospital is 18 minutes away.

Your kit: suction (bulb and catheter), oxygen with infant masks, infant BVM and masks, nebulizer, monitor with capnography, airway roll including infant laryngoscope, tubes and supraglottic airways. No CPAP or high-flow on this unit.
Your partner can ventilate, compress or drive, one at a time.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Watch the trend, not one number: a breathing rate that falls in a tiring infant is not improvement.
Partway through you are asked to explain your reasoning in writing. The case ends at the children's hospital, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Untreated she tires from impending to frank respiratory failure (apnea) in about 6 minutes. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Clearing the nose halves the work of breathing for an obligate nose breather. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Nebulized epinephrine eases the work of breathing by about 30% while it acts. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Effective BVM support lets her rest: fatigue falls about 0.03 per minute. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. An apneic infant desaturates about 0.6% per second. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Below an SpO2 of 70% her heart rate falls about 1.5 beats/min each second; it recovers at 3 per second once oxygenated. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Below 50/min with this hypoxia she is pulseless in this case. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

bvmWord.expr: bvmRate == "none" ? "not in use" : (bvmRate == "right" ? "25 breaths/min, oxygen" : (bvmRate == "slow" ? "12 breaths/min" : "about 50 breaths/min"))

update.fatigue: clamp(bvmOn and bvmRate != "slow" ? fatigue - bvmRest * dt / 60 : fatigue + work * dt / 60, 0.5, 1.2)
update.spo2: spo2 < spo2Target ? min(spo2Target, spo2 + 0.5 * dt) : max(spo2Target, spo2 - desatRate * dt)
update.hr: compressing and bvmOn ? max(hr, 70) : (spo2 < 70 ? max(20, hr - bradyRate * dt) : min(165, hr + 3 * dt))

look.label: Pediatric assessment triangle and primary assessment

then.log: Barely rousable, floppy. Shallow breaths, slower now, head bobbing, grunting; nostrils crusted with mucus. Cool, mottled feet. Her breathing is slowing because she is exhausted.

Appearance: listless, weak cry, does not track. Breathing: fast, grunting, nasal flaring, deep chest retractions, nostrils blocked with thick mucus; crackles and wheeze. Circulation: pale, capillary refill 3 s.

monitor.label: Monitor: pulse oximetry, nasal capnography, ECG

effects.log: Monitor on.

suction.label: Suction the nose and mouth
suction.why: Done; repeat as needed by the parent with the bulb.

effects.log: Thick mucus suctioned from both nostrils; the grunting eases a little.

blowBy.label: Blow-by oxygen held by her mother

effects.log: Blow-by oxygen at 10 L/min.
Infant non-rebreather at 10 L/min.

nebEpi.label: Nebulized epinephrine 5 mg (5 mL of 1 mg/mL)
nebEpi.available: not epiNeb and not nebRunning and not bvmOn
nebEpi.why: Given or running, or she is being ventilated.

effects.log: Nebulized epinephrine running through the infant mask (about 5 min).
No change. In bronchiolitis albuterol is not recommended routinely.
Given. Steroids do not help bronchiolitis.

options.label: 1 breath every 2-3 s (20-30/min), just enough to see the chest rise
1 breath every 5-6 s (10-12/min), the adult rate
As fast as you can squeeze, to get her saturation up

effects.log: Infant mask sealed with an E-C grip, oxygen at 15 L/min, ventilating {rate == "right" ? "about 25 a minute" : (rate == "slow" ? "about 12 a minute" : "as fast as you can")}.
Laryngoscope in. No ventilation during the attempt.

cpr.label: Heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion: compressions 15:2
cpr.why: Only for a heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion despite ventilation.

effects.log: Two-thumb encircling compressions, 15:2 with your partner ventilating.

stopCpr.label: Heart rate back above 60: stop compressions, keep ventilating

effects.log: Compressions stopped; heart rate {hrNow}. Ventilation continues.

transport.label: Load and go to the children's hospital

effects.log: Loading (about 2 min), then 18 minutes. Care continues in the ambulance.
Report: 7-month-old, bronchiolitis with respiratory failure, BVM ventilation, SpO2 {spo2Now}%, HR {hrNow}, ETA.

wait.skipLabel: the end of the nebulizer (about 5 min)

effects.log: Nebulizer finished.

wait.skipLabel: the end of the attempt (about 40 s)

effects.log: Grade 4 view, swollen, secretions everywhere: no tube. Back to the mask; her heart rate has dropped.
At the children's hospital; the team is waiting.
She has stopped breathing.
Heart rate below 60, pale and mottled.
Her belly is tight and distended: air in the stomach, pushing on the diaphragm.
Her breathing is slowing and she no longer cries when touched.

why.question: What told you she was failing rather than improving, and why the bag-valve mask rather than a tube?

parts.label: Recognize and analyze cues
parts.criteria: Listless, weak cry, grunting, retractions, head bobbing, then a breathing rate that slows with falling consciousness and a rising EtCO2: exhaustion and impending respiratory failure, not improvement. Suction (obligate nose breather) and oxygen first; nebulized epinephrine if they fail; albuterol and steroids do not help bronchiolitis.
parts.modelAnswer: She was listless with grunting, retractions and head bobbing, and then her breathing slowed while she got harder to rouse and her EtCO2 climbed: she was tiring out, heading into respiratory failure. Suction her nose, oxygen, nebulized epinephrine if that fails; albuterol and steroids won't help.

parts.label: Take action and evaluate
parts.criteria: Start BVM ventilation for impending failure, 1 breath every 2-3 s with just enough volume to see the chest rise, and reassess SpO2, EtCO2 and heart rate; avoid fast bagging (gastric distension); intubate or place an SGA only if BVM fails; compressions for HR below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
parts.modelAnswer: Bag her at 20-30 a minute, just enough to see the chest rise, and watch SpO2, EtCO2 and the heart rate respond. Bagging fast fills her stomach. The mask was working, so no tube: an infant intubation attempt means no oxygen while you try. If her heart rate stays under 60 with poor perfusion despite good ventilation, start compressions.

noProgress.rationale: She reaches the children's hospital alive but still poorly oxygenated: the support was late or ineffective. This case calls it recovered.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: recognizing failure and choosing BVM

expertPath.text: Assessment triangle: listless, grunting, retractions, pale. Monitor: SpO2 82%, EtCO2 high. Suction both nostrils; non-rebreather.
Still listless and breathing slowing as she tires: impending respiratory failure. BVM with oxygen at 1 breath every 2-3 s, just enough chest rise.
Reassess: SpO2 climbing, EtCO2 falling, HR steady. No tube while the mask works. Load and go.
Radio the children's hospital. Keep ventilating and reassessing all the way.

arrest.headline: Hypoxic arrest
arrest.body: Infants arrest from respiratory failure. A slowing breathing rate in a tiring, listless infant means failure; ventilate before she stops, and never stop ventilating for a tube attempt.

ventilated.headline: Arrived ventilated and pink
ventilated.body: Suction, oxygen, recognizing exhaustion, and a well-sealed mask at 20-30 a minute: the least invasive airway that worked. That is the expert path.

arrivedGaps.headline: Arrived, with gaps
arrivedGaps.body: Look at when ventilation started relative to apnea, the rate you bagged at, and whether a tube attempt cost oxygen.

scoring.modelReasoning: A 7-month-old with three days of cold symptoms, now listless with grunting, retractions, head bobbing, crackles and wheeze, has bronchiolitis with severe distress. Suction the nose and mouth (obligate nose breather) and give oxygen; nebulized epinephrine if they fail; albuterol and steroids do not help. A breathing rate that slows while she becomes harder to rouse and her EtCO2 rises is exhaustion and impending respiratory failure, not improvement: start BVM ventilation with oxygen at 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, with just enough volume to see the chest rise, and reassess SpO2, EtCO2 and heart rate. Fast bagging fills the stomach. Manage the airway the least invasive way that works; an infant intubation attempt stops ventilation. Compress for a heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation. Keep scene time short and notify the children's hospital.

neb.ask: While the nebulizer runs: what will tell you it is not enough?

choices.label: Slowing breaths, harder to rouse, EtCO2 rising
Her breathing rate falling toward normal

neb.explain: In a tiring infant a falling rate, quieter breathing and drowsiness are signs of failure. Reassess frequently; escalate to BVM for impending failure.
